VI. If you are still on the avoided path

content:
Finding Jesus in unexpected places…

Psalm 139:7–10 (ESV)

Where shall I go from your Spirit”
Or where shall I flee from your presence”
If I ascend to heaven, you are there!
If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!
If I take the wings of the morning
and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea,
even there your hand shall lead me,
and your right hand shall hold me.

Some people meet the Lord because they were looking for Him. Many more meet Him because they were not.

They were fleeing. Hiding. Paying fare in the opposite direction. Climbing a tree so they would not have to be seen. Building arguments to keep Him out. Burning His Book. Persecuting His people. Walking away from Jerusalem convinced the story was over.

And He was already standing on that road.

This is not a curiosity of religious biography. It is the character of God. “The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). He does not wait at the end of a well-planned search. He intersects people at the place they chose in order not to meet Him. His mercy runs faster than our flight. His kindness arrives before our apology. His faithfulness holds us in Sheol and on the sea and in the locked room and on the adjacent cross.

If you are reading this while you are still running — or while you are sure He would never come looking for you — these pages are for you.

I. The psalm that will not let you disappear

David does not write Psalm 139 as a threat. He writes it as wonder.

There is no altitude that outclimbs God (v. 8). There is no grave deep enough to bury His presence (v. 8). There is no eastward dawn fast enough to outrun His hand (v. 9). The “uttermost parts of the sea” — Jonah’s geography before Jonah had a book — are already occupied (v. 9–10). Even the darkness we use as cover is not dark to Him (v. 11–12).

And then the psalm turns from flight to formation: “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb” (v. 13). The God we try to escape is the God who made us before we had a path to run. That is why the fleeing never works. We are not running from a stranger. We are running from the One whose eyes saw our unformed substance (v. 16).

Hosea hears the same heart in the voice of God over a nation that would not stay: “How can I give you up, O Ephraim” … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender” (Hosea 11:8). Ezekiel hears the Shepherd’s job description: “I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). Jesus puts it in one sentence that explains His whole ministry: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

Paul later names the timing: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Not after we became likely. Not after we turned around. While.

What follows is not a catalogue for its own sake. It is a cloud of witnesses — twenty-two from Scripture, twelve from later centuries — that the mercy of God has a habit of standing in the road we took to leave.

II. Twenty-two times Scripture records the avoided path

Each scene has the same three beats: the path they chose in order to avoid Him, the place He met them, and the mercy that would not let them go.

Flight and the opposite direction

1. Adam and Eve among the trees (Genesis 3:8–9)
The first human instinct after sin is concealment. They hide from the sound of the Lord walking in the garden. God does not wait for them to come out. He seeks: “Where are you”” The first question God asks fallen humanity is not a prosecution. It is a pursuit.

2. Jonah toward Tarshish (Jonah 1–2)
Commanded east to Nineveh, he pays fare west “from the presence of the Lord.” The storm he hoped would hide him becomes the pulpit. The fish he never chose becomes the chapel. Mercy uses the avoided sea to turn the prophet around.

3. Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:10–22)
He runs after deceiving Isaac and stealing Esau’s blessing. A stone for a pillow. No altar. No repentance speech. God opens heaven over the fugitive and renews the covenant. The place of flight is named Bethel — house of God.

4. Jacob at Peniel (Genesis 32:22–32)
Twenty years later he is still managing, still afraid, still sending gifts ahead to buy safety. Alone at the Jabbok at night, he is met and wrestled until daybreak. The man running from consequence is given a new name: Israel.

5. Moses at Horeb (Exodus 2:15; 3:1–6)
A murdered Egyptian, a wanted man, forty years of anonymous shepherding on “the far side of the wilderness.” The bush burns not at Pharaoh’s court but on the path Moses took to disappear. The voice that calls him is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — still faithful after forty hidden years.

6. Balaam on the road to curse Israel (Numbers 22:21–35)
Hired to speak against God’s people, he goes even after the warning. An angel with a drawn sword blocks the path the prophet cannot see. The donkey sees what the seer will not. God meets the man on the errand he should never have accepted, and turns intended curse into blessing.

7. The Emmaus disciples walking away from Jerusalem (Luke 24:13–35)
They leave the city of the cross convinced the story is finished. Jesus walks the road of their disillusionment unrecognized, opens Moses and the Prophets, and is known in the breaking of bread. He does not wait in Jerusalem for them to return. He goes with them in the wrong direction.

Hiding, isolation, and the unusual hour

8. Hagar on the road to Shur (Genesis 16:6–13)
Pregnant, mistreated, she flees into the wilderness. The Angel of the Lord finds her by a spring. She names Him El Roi — the God who sees. A second time, sent away with Ishmael (Genesis 21), God hears the boy’s cry in the desert. The slave woman on the run becomes the first person in Scripture to name God from her own encounter.

9. Gideon in the winepress (Judges 6:11–16)
Threshing wheat in a hole meant for grapes, hiding the harvest from Midian. The Angel of the Lord sits down under the oak and addresses the hidden man as “mighty warrior.” The call comes in the place of concealment, not on a battlefield.

10. Elijah in the cave at Horeb (1 Kings 19:3–18)
After Carmel he runs a day’s journey into the desert, asks to die, and hides in a cave. God is not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire. The whisper finds the prophet who has quit. Recommissioning happens in the hiding place.

11. The Samaritan woman at noon (John 4:4–26)
She comes at the hour when no respectable woman draws water, to avoid the well of public shame. Jesus “had to pass through Samaria” and is already sitting at the well. Living water is offered not in the synagogue at the hour of prayer, but at the avoided well at the avoided time.

12. Zacchaeus in the sycamore (Luke 19:1–10)
A despised tax collector climbs a tree to see without being seen. Jesus stops under that tree, calls him by name, and invites Himself to the house the town would not enter. “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” is spoken over a man who was trying not to be found.

13. The Gerasene among the tombs (Mark 5:1–20)
Naked, self-harming, living in exile on a pagan shore. Jesus crosses a storm to get to him. Deliverance happens in the graveyard the man cannot leave, not after he has cleaned himself up and come to town.

14. Nicodemus by night (John 3:1–21)
A Pharisee comes under cover of darkness to avoid the cost of being seen with Jesus. The conversation about new birth happens in the shadows he chose. Later he will come in daylight with spices for the body (John 19:39). Night was not a barrier. It was the appointed hour.

Hostility, shame, and the locked room

15. Saul on the Damascus road (Acts 9:1–19)
Not seeking Christ. Hunting the church. Letters in hand, breathing threats. The light and the voice — “Why are you persecuting Me”” — meet him on the road of persecution itself. The church’s chief enemy becomes its apostle on the exact path of his violence.

16. The woman caught in adultery (John 8:2–11)
Dragged into the temple as a trap, exposed, awaiting stones. Jesus stoops into her shame, writes on the ground, and when the accusers leave He remains. “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” He meets her at the point of public ruin.

17. The thief on the cross (Luke 23:39–43)
A dying criminal, not a seeker. Hours from death, no time for reform. Jesus is beside him on the adjacent cross — the last place anyone would look for God — and opens paradise that day. Mercy’s last word on Golgotha is spoken to a man who had no future left to offer.

18. Thomas in the locked room (John 20:24–29)
The others have seen the risen Lord. Thomas refuses their report and stays inside his conditions. Jesus comes through the locked door eight days later and offers the wounds Thomas demanded. The skeptic’s terms become the place of worship: “My Lord and my God.”

19. Mary Magdalene at the tomb (John 20:11–18)
She is looking for a corpse, not a living Lord. Grief has her facing the wrong direction. She mistakes Him for the gardener. He speaks her name. The first witness of the resurrection is a woman who came expecting only death.

20. Peter at the charcoal fire (John 21:1–19)
After denial he goes back to fishing — the old trade, the old boat. Jesus is already on the shore with a charcoal fire, the same kind of fire at which Peter denied Him. Breakfast before reinstatement. “Do you love Me”” is asked on the beach Peter chose as an exit.

21. The Philippian jailer (Acts 16:25–34)
Earthquake, open doors, he draws his sword to kill himself rather than face Roman disgrace. Paul shouts from the dark: “Do not harm yourself.” The man about to die by his own hand asks, “What must I do to be saved”” Salvation arrives in the prison at the edge of suicide.

22. Manasseh in Babylonian chains (2 Chronicles 33:10–13)
Judah’s most defiant king — child sacrifice, occult, blood in Jerusalem — is taken with hooks and bronze fetters to Babylon. “When he was in distress, he implored the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly.” God hears him in the prison of his own making and restores him. Then Manasseh knows that the Lord is God.

Jesus tells the same story as a parable of the Father. The prodigal is still “a long way off,” coming from the pigsty, rehearsing a speech, when the father runs (Luke 15:20). The son’s return path is met before it is completed. That is not sentiment. That is the gospel in one motion.

III. Twelve later witnesses on the same road

Scripture is sufficient. These names are not a second canon. They are simply what happens when the God of Psalm 139 keeps doing what He has always done. Each account is public, named, and written down.

1. Augustine of Hippo (354–430)
He wanted truth on his own terms and delayed holiness: “Give me chastity and continence, but not yet.” In a garden in Milan he heard a child chanting tolle lege — take up and read — opened Romans 13, and was found. Confessions is the record of a man chased down by mercy.

2. John Newton (1725–1807)
Slave-ship captain, blasphemer, morally collapsed. In a storm at sea in 1748, reading Thomas à Kempis, the man fleeing every restraint was found. He would later write the hymn that is itself a testimony: “I once was lost, but now am found.” Amazing grace is not a mood. It is Newton’s biography.

3. Sadhu Sundar Singh (1889–1929)
A Sikh youth in Punjab who blamed the Christian God for his mother’s death. He tore a Bible apart and burned it page by page. Three days later, planning to throw himself under the morning train if God did not reveal Himself, he prayed through the night of 18 December 1904. A light filled the room. He expected Krishna or Buddha. He saw the crucified Christ, and heard in Hindustani the Damascus question: “Why do you persecute Me”” The boy who burned the Book became the sadhu with bleeding feet, walking India and Tibet with the Name he had tried to erase.

4. C. S. Lewis (1898–1963)
Oxford atheist, constructing arguments to keep God at bay. In Surprised by Joy he describes 1929: he “gave in, and admitted that God was God,” “the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England,” kneeling in his rooms at Magdalen. He later recognized the old poem’s line as his own story — the Hound of Heaven.

5. Charles Colson (1931–2012)
Nixon’s “hatchet man.” In 1973, with Watergate collapsing around him, he sat in a friend’s house and read Lewis’s Mere Christianity. Prison followed. So did Prison Fellowship. Born Again is the record of a man found at the end of power.

6. Lee Strobel (b. 1952)
Yale-trained legal journalist at the Chicago Tribune, atheist. When his wife Leslie became a Christian he set out to disprove the faith and “rescue” her from a cult. Two years of investigation into the resurrection ended on 8 November 1981 with a conclusion he did not want: it would take more faith to remain an atheist. The Case for Christ is an investigation aimed the wrong way.

7. J. Warner Wallace
Cold-case homicide detective, lifelong atheist. He applied forensic statement analysis to the Gospels intending to treat them as claims to be broken. He became convinced they read as early eyewitness testimony. Conversion around 1996. Cold-Case Christianity is what happens when the detective cannot close the case against the risen Lord.

8. Rosaria Butterfield
Tenured Syracuse professor of English and Queer Theory, writing against the Religious Right. She accepted a pastor’s dinner invitation as research. Scripture undid the project. The Secret Thoughts of an Unlikely Convert tells how hospitality became the road she had not meant to walk.

9. Nabeel Qureshi (1983–2017)
A devout Ahmadi Muslim who studied for years to refute the resurrection and win Christians to Islam. The evidence he assembled to destroy the claim convinced him of it. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus is the account of a refutation that failed upward into worship.

10. David Wood
Militant atheist, imprisoned after a violent crime. He argued with a Christian inmate in order to defeat him, and began reading Scripture to win the argument. He converted in prison in 1996. He was not seeking God. He was trying to beat a Christian at debate. The Book he opened as a weapon opened him.

11. Bilquis Sheikh (1912–1997)
A prominent Pakistani Muslim woman of Wah, wife of a former interior minister, living in a walled garden after her marriage ended. Dreams she did not request — dining with Jesus, meeting John the Baptist — drove her to a Bible she was not supposed to read. A Catholic sister told her to talk to God as to her own father. On 24 December 1966 she did. I Dared to Call Him Father is the record of a woman who found that the God of Islam’s distance had a name she had never been permitted to use: Father.

12. Gulshan Esther (Gulshan Fatima)
Youngest daughter of a Sayed family in Jhang, Punjab; in purdah; crippled from infancy and confined to her room for nineteen years. After her father’s death she stopped using set prayer and began to speak to God as One who knew her. She heard the voice of Jesus son of Mary. When He told her to stand, she — who could not stand — stood. The Torn Veil is her testimony that the veil of inherited religion was torn, not by her climbing, but by His appearing.

Twelve different centuries, languages, and wounds. One pattern. He does not require that we find the road to Him. He stands on the road we took to leave.

IV. What kind of God does this”

Not a God who is merely powerful. A God whose power is yoked to mercy.

Merciful — He does not treat Adam’s hiding, Jonah’s ticket, Saul’s letters, or Sundar’s burning of the Book as the last word. “He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10).

Kind — The Samaritan woman is not exposed at noon; she is offered water. Zacchaeus is not lectured from the road; he is invited to the table. Peter is not handed a list of failures; he is handed breakfast. “When the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared…” (Titus 3:4).

Faithful — Forty years in Midian do not cancel the burning bush. Twenty years of Jacob’s managing do not cancel Peniel. Manasseh’s decades of defiance do not cancel the prayer in Babylon. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

Patient — He lets Thomas keep the locked door for eight days and then comes through it. He lets Elijah finish the collapse in the cave and then whispers. “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise… but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

Seeking — “I myself will search for my sheep.” The initiative is almost never ours. The gospel is not the story of humanity finding God. It is the story of God finding humanity, at cost to Himself.

That cost is the center. Every avoided path in this list leans toward one hill. The Cross is the ultimate unexpected place: God meets us on the ground we used to get rid of Him. The thief’s adjacent cross is that pattern in a single afternoon. The torn veil of the temple (Matthew 27:51) and the torn veil of Gulshan’s title are not two different mercies. They are one mercy, reaching a dying criminal and a crippled girl in Jhang and a professor in Syracuse and a detective in California and whoever is reading this while still facing the other way.

V. What this is not

It is not permission to keep running.

Jonah is still sent to Nineveh. Moses still has to stand before Pharaoh. Saul still has to enter the city blind and wait for Ananias. Sundar still has to leave his father’s house with nothing but the clothes on his back. Finding is unto turning. Grace that only comforts and never commands is not the grace of the New Testament.

It is not a promise that every flight will feel like a vision. Most of these meetings were unwelcome at first. Moses hid his face. Jonah was furious. Lewis was dejected. Bilquis was frightened by a Presence in her garden. The kindness of God is not the same thing as the convenience of God.

It is not a technique. You cannot game the Hound of Heaven by running farther in hopes of a better story. “Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance”” (Romans 2:4).

VI. If you are still on the avoided path

Then you are, strangely, in the most crowded company in Scripture.

You may be hiding among trees of shame. Paying fare away from a call you do not want. Sitting at a well at the hour no one else comes. Climbing so as not to be named. Walking away from a crucifixion you have decided is final. Building a case against a Book. Burning what you cannot bear to read. Holding a sword against your own life.

Psalm 139 has already mapped the territory. Heaven, Sheol, the wings of the morning, the uttermost sea, the darkness you think is cover — even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me.

You do not have to find the language. Hagar had no liturgy; she named Him after He found her. The thief had no time; he had a sentence. The jailer had a question: “What must I do to be saved”” The answer has not changed: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31).

He is not waiting for you to become findable. He is already on the road.

Psalm 139:23–24 (ESV)

Search me, O God, and know my heart!
Try me and know my thoughts!
And see if there be any grievous way in me,
and lead me in the way everlasting.

The psalm that began with “where shall I flee”” ends with “search me.” That is what happens when the fleeing soul discovers that the One it was running from is the only One who can lead it home.

El Roi sees you. The Father runs. The Son sits at the avoided well. The Spirit will not leave you in the dark you chose.

Come.

Scripture quotations are from the ESV. Modern accounts are drawn from the subjects’ own published testimonies and standard biographies: Augustine, Confessions; Newton’s Authentic Narrative and “Amazing Grace”; Sundar Singh’s recorded vision of December 1904; Lewis, Surprised by Joy; Colson, Born Again; Strobel, The Case for Christ; Wallace, Cold-Case Christianity; Butterfield, The Secret Thoughts of an Unlikely Convert; Qureshi, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus; Wood’s published prison testimony; Sheikh, I Dared to Call Him Father; Esther, The Torn Veil.

What Christianity Helped Abolish in India

Colonial Interference or Social Evils That Were Named, Opposed, and Destroyed

Sequel to Part 1: Pray for India  ·  August 2026← Part 2: Heritage of Faithful Service — Builders of Literacy and Medicine

“He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed.” — Luke 4:18 (ESV)

The preceding chapters of this series recorded what Christianity built in India: the schools, the colleges, the hospitals, the printing presses, the nursing programmes, the leprosy homes. This chapter records what Christianity destroyed — the practices, institutionalised across centuries, that consumed the bodies and lives of the weakest members of Indian society. Widows. Children. Girls dedicated to temples. Travellers on the roads. Tribal infants offered to the earth. First-born daughters drowned in milk. Low-caste women stripped of the right to clothe themselves.

These were not fringe aberrations. They were embedded in religion, economy, caste structure, and custom. They were defended by priests, tolerated by administrators, and sanctioned by centuries of practice. In every case, the first sustained opposition came from Christians — missionaries who named them, recorded them, campaigned against them, sheltered their victims, and refused to yield until the law changed. The record is not a matter of interpretation. It is documented in petitions, in parliamentary debates, in the founding legislation of a reforming colonial government, and in the institutions that persist to this day.

What follows is the chronological account of each evil, the persons who opposed it, and the year it was officially ended — knowing that legislation is not always the same as eradication, and that several of these battles were not won cleanly or finally. They were won at cost.

Learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow’s cause.Isaiah 1:17 (ESV)

At a Glance — The Catalogue of Abolished Evils

The Chronological Record

Evil I · Circa 5th–9th Century AD onward

Sati — सती

The burning of widows alive upon the funeral pyre of their husbands

1829 Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII) — Governor-General Lord William Bentinck

In the spring of 1799, William Carey was riding near Malda in Bengal when he came upon a scene he would never forget. A widow — young, and in the description of those present, apparently not acting freely — was being prepared for the pyre of her dead husband. Carey attempted to intervene, to reason with the Brahmin priests, to speak with the woman. He was told to stand back. “I talked till reasoning was of no use,” he later wrote, “and then began to exclaim with all my might against what they were doing; telling them it was shocking murder. They told me it was a great act of holiness.”

What he witnessed that evening was not exceptional. In the year 1817 alone, some 700 widows were burned alive around Calcutta. Carey’s own investigators, sent into every village within thirty miles, documented nearly 300 deaths in a single year in that region. Across all of India, he estimated more than 10,000 such deaths annually. He personally documented a single case in which 33 wives of one man were burned together at his funeral.

Carey spent the next thirty years in sustained, methodical opposition. He studied the Vedas and the Sanskrit Shastras for months in order to argue — on Hindu scriptural grounds — that sati had no textual basis in the authoritative texts of Hinduism itself. His former pundit, by 1816 the chief pundit of the Supreme Court of Calcutta, reached the same conclusion. Carey and his colleagues at Serampore — Joshua Marshman and William Ward — compiled statistics of victims, published indictments in the Friend of India and Samachar Darpan, submitted formal petitions to the colonial government, and wrote to Members of Parliament in Britain. When the British government moved to dismiss the evidence, the missionaries produced more. When it claimed sati was voluntary, the missionaries published accounts of women who had been dragged, drugged, or pinned with bamboo poles to the pyre. William Wilberforce himself, fresh from the abolition of the slave trade, joined Carey’s advocacy in the British Parliament.

In 1828, Lord William Bentinck was appointed Governor-General. A man of active Christian conviction, Bentinck had already determined that the practice must end. He consulted widely — Indian leaders, British administrators, the missionaries — and on 4 December 1829 promulgated Bengal Sati Regulation XVII: the practice of Sati or of burning or burying alive the widows of Hindus is hereby declared illegal and punishable by the criminal courts. Carey received the translation task that morning. He set aside his Sunday sermon, sat down, and translated the regulation into Bengali that day, so that it could be published across the province without an hour’s delay. It was, as the Serampore missionaries called it, “a bold and decisive step.” It had taken thirty years.

Primary Agents

  • William Carey (1761–1834) — First witness, chief campaigner; 30-year sustained advocacy; Sanskrit textual research
  • Joshua Marshman & William Ward — Serampore Trio; publication, statistics, petitions
  • Lord William Bentinck (1774–1839) — Practicing Christian; promulgated the abolition regulation
  • William Wilberforce (1759–1833) — Parliamentary advocate alongside Carey from Britain
  • James Peggs — Baptist; published India’s Cries to British Humanity, forcing Parliamentary attention

Evil II · Ancient — systematic from Rajput era

Doodh Peeti — दूध पीती

Drowning newborn daughters in pots of milk; female infanticide across multiple regions and methods

1870 Female Infanticide Prevention Act — enacted under pressure from Christian missionary advocacy

In 1794, barely a year after his arrival in India, William Carey and his colleague John Thomas were riding near Malda when they discovered a basket hung in a tree. Inside were the skull and partial remains of an infant. The basket had been placed there as an act of religious devotion — the deliberate exposure of a newborn child, considered a sacred sacrifice. It was not an isolated sight. Across the Rajput communities of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Saurashtra, and Kutch, the birth of a daughter was regarded as an economic catastrophe: the dowry demands of the future were considered ruinous enough to justify killing the child at birth. The preferred method among the Jadeja Rajput clans was doodh peeti — the infant girl was drowned in a pot or trough of cow’s milk, a euphemism that turned murder into a ritual of feeding. A British census in 1805 found almost no surviving girls in the Jadeja Rajput families of Kutch and Kathiawar.

The practice was not confined to Gujarat. Across the subcontinent — in the hills of Bengal, in the Gangetic plain, in Punjab — girl children were exposed, suffocated, or abandoned at birth at rates that colonial surveyors found difficult to document because the evidence was designed to disappear. The East India Company’s instinct was not to interfere in religious custom. The missionaries disagreed. From the early nineteenth century onward, Carey and the Serampore community sent investigators to document the deaths, published their findings in the Friend of India, submitted petitions to the government, and argued — as they had argued against sati — that this was murder wearing a religious mask, and that the mask did not make it anything other than murder.

Baptist pastor James Peggs gave the campaign a pamphlet of moral force in his India’s Cries to British Humanity, which documented female infanticide alongside sati and the Juggernaut deaths and demanded parliamentary action. The colonial government, moved by sustained missionary pressure and increasingly embarrassed by the statistical evidence that the missionaries had compiled, passed the Female Infanticide Prevention Act in 1870, applying to Oudh, the North-Western Provinces, and Punjab, with provision for extension across British India.

Primary Agents

  • William Carey — First systematic documentation; petitioned government in 1802
  • James Peggs — Baptist; campaigning publication; sustained parliamentary pressure
  • Baptist Missionary Society press — Friend of India and Samachar Darpan sustained public record

Evil III · Ancient custom — reform campaign from 1880s

Bal Vivah — बाल विवाह

The marriage of girls as young as seven or eight; consummation inflicted upon children who had not reached puberty

1891 / 1929 Age of Consent Act 1891 (raised consent to age 12); Child Marriage Restraint Act (Sarda Act) 1929 (minimum age 14 girls / 18 boys)

The case that broke the silence was that of Phulmoni Dasi — a child bride of ten or eleven years in Bengal who died in 1889 after her adult husband forced marital consummation upon her. The case became public because the husband was tried for grievous bodily harm. He was convicted. But the legal age of consent for married women was at that point ten years old, meaning that what he had done was not, strictly speaking, criminal under the law as it stood. The public outcry in Britain was immediate. The legal obscenity — that a man could kill a child through marital rape without committing a crime in the technical sense — forced Parliament’s hand.

It was Christian missionaries who had been naming this practice as evil for the better part of the century before Phulmoni Dasi’s death forced the issue into the open. The Zenana missions — women missionaries working inside the private quarters of Indian households, where male missionaries could not go — had been documenting the physical consequences of child marriage for decades: the torn bodies of girls who had not yet developed, the deaths in childbed of mothers no older than thirteen, the lives consumed before they had properly begun. These women wrote. They reported. Their reports accumulated in mission society journals and in the campaigns of figures like William Carey, who had petitioned the government on child marriage as early as 1802 in the same letters in which he documented sati and infanticide.

Pandita Ramabai — Brahmin by birth, Sanskrit scholar, convert to Christianity in 1891 — became the most powerful Indian voice against both child marriage and its most frequent consequence: enforced widowhood. Her book The High-Caste Hindu Woman, published in 1887 and read across Britain and America, set out in plain terms what happened to girls married before puberty and widowed before they were adults. Indian Christian women signed petitions to the Governor-General in 1891 supporting the Age of Consent Bill — among 128 Parsi and 83 native Christian women from Pune alone — while orthodox Hindu leaders, including Bal Gangadhar Tilak, opposed it strenuously on grounds of religious autonomy. The Bill became law in 1891 but raised the age only to twelve, a reform considered timid by many. The Sarda Act of 1929 raised the minimum age for girls to fourteen. Full reform came only post-Independence.

Primary Agents

  • Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) — Sanskrit scholar, convert to Christianity 1891; The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887); founder Mukti Mission; personally rescued thousands of child widows
  • Zenana mission women — Church of England Zenana Missionary Society and CMS; documented physical harm; advocacy in private quarters of Indian homes
  • Indian Christian women petitioners — 83 native Christian women of Pune signed the 1891 petition to the Governor-General in support of the Bill
  • William Carey — Early petitioner (1802) linking child marriage to infanticide and sati

“Something must be done.”— Elisabeth Elliot, quoting Amy Carmichael on first seeing the Devadasi system, A Chance to Die (1987)

Evil IV · Ancient — pre-medieval in origin

Devadasi — देवदासी

“Servant of the god” — the dedication of girls, sometimes from infancy, to Hindu deities/temple priestess’ as perpetual ritual sex slaves

1947 / 1948 Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act, 9 October 1947 — Tamil Nadu. Pan-India enforcement remained incomplete for decades.

In March 1901, Amy Carmichael received a child. The girl’s name was Preena. She was seven years old. She had been sold by her widowed mother to a Hindu temple in the village of Pannaivilai — dedicated to the deity as a devadasi, a “servant of god.” In practice this meant that she was the sexual property of the temple priests and their patrons, available from the time her body permitted it, and for the rest of her life. She had already been branded on the hand for a previous attempt to escape. She had come to Carmichael because she had heard that the foreign woman might shelter her.

Carmichael sheltered her. And then she began to understand, in full detail, what the devadasi system was. Girls — some as young as three or four — were purchased or donated by families too poor to refuse the temple’s payment, or convinced that dedication to the deity was a spiritual honour. Once inside the system, they were trained in music and dance, married ritually to the god, and made available to the priests and to wealthy temple patrons. They could never leave the temple service. They could never marry a human husband. The system was ancient, it was organised, it was protected by religious authority, and it operated in temples across Tamil Nadu, Andhra, Karnataka, and Maharashtra, involving hundreds of thousands of girls and women.

Carmichael named it — directly, unflinchingly, at a time when such directness was considered improper. Her book Things as They Are (1903) described the system in as much detail as Victorian publishing conventions would allow, and more than enough to cause outrage among her readers in Britain and Ireland. She rescued children herself, often traveling long distances through the Tamil heat, sometimes in disguise — she dressed in a sari and stained her skin, and thanked God throughout her life for the brown eyes that had seemed a disappointment in childhood but now allowed her to move where fair-skinned missionaries could not. She faced charges of kidnapping and spent years under legal threat. She endured the accusation from other missionaries that her methods were sensational, her claims exaggerated. She continued.

By the time of her death in 1951, the Dohnavur Fellowship had sheltered and raised more than a thousand children rescued from the temple system. The Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act had been enacted in October 1947, making temple dedication illegal across the Madras Presidency. The campaigning that produced that legislation was directly traceable — through Indian Christian advocacy and the documentation that Amy Carmichael had spent fifty years accumulating — to the work of the Dohnavur Fellowship and the Tamil Christian community.

Primary Agents

  • Amy Carmichael (1867–1951) — Founded Dohnavur Fellowship 1901; rescued 1,000+ children; Things as They Are (1903); sustained advocacy for 50 years without furlough
  • The Dohnavur Fellowship community — Indian women co-workers who formed the rescue network
  • Mayuram Vedanayakam Pillai (1826–1889) — Tamil Christian lyricist; anti-devadasi writing in vernacular Tamil literature, predating Carmichael by decades

Evil V · Medieval in origin — systematic for at least four centuries

Thuggee — ठगी

The ritual strangling of travellers as an act of devotion to the goddess Kali — organised, generational, hereditary criminal fraternities

1835–1840s Thuggee and Dacoity Department established 1835; networks dismantled by early 1840s. Over 3,000 Thugs arrested 1831–1837.

The men who strangled travellers on the roads of India were not bandits in the ordinary sense. They were the inheritors of a hereditary craft passed from father to son across generations, governed by precise ritual protocol, and understood by its practitioners as a religious obligation. A Thug did not kill for money alone — though the plunder of victims supported the organisation. He killed as an act of worship to Kali, the goddess of death and destruction, offering her the body of the strangled victim and giving her the coin of sacrifice from the spoils. The rumal — the strangling cloth, typically a yellow silk handkerchief — was the sacred instrument, and its use was governed by rules as specific as those of any other ritual.

Estimates of the death toll are difficult to establish, but the operations of the Thuggee networks across central India over several centuries likely claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. Whole caravans — groups of twenty, thirty, fifty travellers — could be infiltrated, befriended over days of shared road travel, and massacred in a single coordinated attack. The bodies were buried in pre-dug graves, the possessions distributed, and the company of Thugs dispersed before any alarm could be raised. The East India Company had known of the phenomenon for decades and done little. The political cost of interfering in what appeared to be a religious practice was considered too high.

Lord William Bentinck — the same practicing Christian who had abolished sati in 1829 — refused the calculation. In 1830, under his direction, Captain William Henry Sleeman was appointed to lead a campaign of systematic intelligence-gathering, infiltration, and prosecution. Bentinck established the Thuggee and Dacoity Department formally in 1835, with Sleeman as its superintendent. The Christian moral framework that had driven Bentinck to end sati drove him equally on Thuggee: no religious sanction, however ancient, licensed murder. Within a decade the networks were dismantled. More than 3,000 Thugs were arrested between 1831 and 1837. The practice was effectively destroyed as an organised system by the early 1840s.

Primary Agents

  • Lord William Bentinck — Practicing Christian; political will and executive authority; established the Thuggee Department
  • Col. William Henry Sleeman — Commander of suppression operations from 1830; Ramaseeana (1836); later Commissioner for Suppression of Thuggee and Dacoity
  • Missionary press — Documentation and sustained advocacy that kept Parliamentary attention on organised crime with religious sanction

Evil VI · Ancient — documented from at least the 17th century AD

Meriah — मेरिया

The ritual human sacrifice of purchased victims — men, women, and children — to the earth goddess Tana Penu / Darni Penu by the Kondh (Kandha) tribal peoples of Odisha

1854 (formal suppression) Meriah Agency established by Government of India Act XXI, 1845. Formal eradication declared 1854; 1,506 victims rescued 1837–1854.

The Meriah sacrifice was among the most elaborately organised forms of institutionalised killing in the history of the Indian subcontinent. The Kondh tribes of the Kandhamal region in Odisha — a remote and densely forested hill country that the British administration reached only gradually — maintained a practice in which human victims, known as Meriah, were purchased in childhood from famine-stricken communities across the region and raised within Kondh villages over months or years before being sacrificed to the earth goddess to ensure agricultural fertility. The Meriah was treated well during his captivity — fed, housed, sometimes given a wife — because the quality of the sacrifice was believed to determine the quality of the harvest.

On the appointed day, the victim was given large quantities of liquor to diminish awareness of what was happening, and then killed by a method that varied by sub-tribe: sometimes dismemberment, sometimes burial alive, sometimes crushing. The body was divided among the participating villages and the pieces buried in the fields.

The British administration’s initial surveys of the Kondh country in the 1830s revealed the practice to officials who had not previously encountered it at this scale. The Meriah Agency was formally established under Government of India Act XXI of 1845, with Captain John Campbell appointed as its first superintendent with the explicit mandate to suppress human sacrifice across the Khond territories. Campbell’s colleague Major Samuel Charters Macpherson worked alongside him in the Kandhamal region, negotiating with tribal chiefs, offering alternative ceremonies, and directly intervening to rescue Meriah victims before their sacrifice dates. Between 1837 and 1854, the agents of the Meriah Agency rescued a documented 1,506 victims — men, women, and children who would otherwise have been killed. Dr. John Buckley, a missionary working in Odisha during the same period, estimated the total rescued, including through missionary activity, at closer to 1,700.

The Kondh were not passive recipients of colonial interference — armed resistance was frequent, and the work of the Meriah agents was carried on under conditions of genuine physical danger. Over time, persuasion and the provision of buffalo as a substitute sacrifice — the practice known as Kedu — brought gradual change. The formal declaration of suppression in 1854 was not the same as eradication: isolated instances persisted in remote areas into the 1880s and beyond. But the organised, inter-village, market-supported system of purchasing human victims for sacrifice had been broken.

Primary Agents

  • Captain John Campbell — First Meriah Agent; thirteen years of service; published Personal Narrative of Thirteen Years’ Service among the Wild Tribes of Khondistan (1864)
  • Major Samuel Charters Macpherson — Field operations; rescued 255 Meriah victims personally
  • Dr. John Buckley — Missionary in Odisha; estimated 1,700 total rescues; education advocacy for freed Meriah victims
  • Amos Sutton — General Baptist missionary, Cuttack (from 1822); first English grammar of Odia; foundational missionary presence that enabled later Meriah-region work

Evil VII · Ancient Shaivite ritual — petitioned against from the 1800s

Hook-Swinging (Charak Puja) — चरक पूजा

Devotees suspended from iron hooks pierced through the skin of their backs, swung in circles at height as a religious offering to Shiva

1856 (Bengal) Prohibited in Bengal 1856; curtailed in Madras by earlier administrative orders; partly restricted but never fully eliminated across all territories.

The Charak Puja festival of Bengal and the self-mortification practices associated with it represented a category of religious harm that fell below the threshold of death in most cases — which made it simultaneously easier to ignore and harder to argue against. Devotees at the springtime festival of Shiva would submit to the insertion of iron hooks through the skin of their backs and be lifted into the air on ropes, swung in circles before crowds of thousands, as an act of religious devotion and petition. Other practices at the same festival included walking on burning coals, jumping onto open blades, and rolling across circles of thorns. The participants were often in states of religious trance or intoxication that diminished their awareness of the physical trauma.

William Carey and other missionaries petitioned the British administration in the early decades of the nineteenth century, describing the practice as “cruel and degrading, without having any religious sanction.” Christian missionaries and English-educated Indian committees alike brought representations to the Commissioner of Police and to district Superintendents of Police. The administration was slow to act — the political sensitivity of restricting public religious practice remained acute. Hook-swinging was prohibited in Bengal in 1856. The Madras administration took earlier administrative action against the most injurious forms of the practice, without full formal prohibition. Sadly, the festival in various modified forms persisted in private spaces, and the Thaipusam festival among Tamil Hindu communities continues body-suspension practices to the present.

Primary Agents

  • William Carey — Petitioner against hook-swinging as one of a cluster of practices involving religious self-harm
  • Missionary committees in Calcutta and Madras — Formal petitions to British administrators through the early 19th century

Evil VIII · Ancient caste custom — revolt 1813–1859

Caste Nudity — The Breast Tax

Low-caste women in Travancore (Kerala) were legally prohibited from covering their breasts — a mark of submission to higher castes; women who covered themselves faced fines and violence

1859 Royal Proclamation of the Maharaja of Travancore, 26 July 1859 — all women of the Nadar (Channar/Shanar) community granted the right to wear upper garments, under pressure from British Governor-General and Christian advocacy.

The custom was not metaphorical. In the princely state of Travancore in what is now Kerala, women of the lower castes — particularly the Nadar (Channar/Shanar) community, whose traditional occupation was toddy-tapping from palmyra trees — were legally prohibited from covering the upper portion of their bodies in public. To do so was to claim a social status that the caste hierarchy denied them. Upper-caste Nair and Brahmin custom enforced the rule: a lower-caste woman who covered her breasts could be assaulted, fined, or stripped by members of dominant castes who chose to enforce it. The humiliation was deliberate and systematic, a constant bodily reminder of their position at the bottom of the social order.

When London Missionary Society missionaries began working among the Nadar community in the early nineteenth century, they did something that immediately became a flashpoint: they gave their female converts blouses to wear as part of their Christian dress. This was not a cultural imposition — it was an act of dignity. The converts wore them. Upper-caste Nairs attacked them. Violence erupted across the region repeatedly between 1813 and 1859. Missionaries were assaulted. Churches were burned. Women were forcibly stripped of their garments in the streets.

Colonel John Munro, the Diwan of Travancore and a practicing Christian, issued an administrative order in 1814 granting Christian Nadar women the right to cover themselves — acknowledging the anomaly that conversion was the only mechanism by which a woman could claim a basic right over her own body. The compromise was imperfect and the violence continued. It was only on 26 July 1859, under sustained pressure from Charles Trevelyan, the Madras Governor, and with decades of missionary advocacy behind it, that the Maharaja of Travancore issued a proclamation extending the right of dress to all Nadar women regardless of religious affiliation. It had taken forty-six years of protest and suffering to achieve what other human beings accepted as a natural condition of existence.

Primary Christian Agents

  • London Missionary Society missionaries — Gave blouses to female converts; sustained presence alongside Nadar Christian community through forty-six years of conflict
  • Colonel John Munro (Diwan of Travancore, practicing Christian) — 1814 administrative order extending dress rights to Christian Nadar women
  • Nadar Christian converts themselves — Women who wore the garments at personal risk, whose repeated public assertion of the right created the political pressure
  • Charles Trevelyan (Madras Governor) — Applied the decisive pressure that produced the 1859 Royal Proclamation

Evil IX · Ancient — codified in Dharmaśāstra traditions

Enforced Widowhood — विधवा प्रथा

as depicted in Water

The social death imposed on widows: head-shaving, isolation, starvation rations, prohibition of remarriage, and permanent ritual impurity — often imposed on girls widowed before puberty

1856 (legal right to remarry) Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act, 1856. Social practice of enforced widowhood continued long after and was addressed through Mukti Mission rescue work.

The custom of enforced widowhood was the shadow side of child marriage. A girl married at seven who was widowed at ten — her husband having died of the diseases that carried off young men in nineteenth-century India at formidable rates — faced a future of such severity that death was sometimes regarded as preferable to it. Her head was shaved. She was given one plain white garment. She was placed on starvation rations, confined to the house, excluded from family celebrations, festivals, and meals. She was a permanent ritual pollutant — her very presence at an auspicious occasion was considered an ill omen. She could never remarry. She would remain in this condition, locked inside the family home as a source of unpaid domestic labour, until she died. If she was young enough and destitute enough, she might be sold to a temple.

Pandita Ramabai had seen this system from the inside. Her Brahmin family had been ruined in a famine. She had watched her parents and her sister die of starvation. She had been widowed young herself. She understood — from her mastery of the Sanskrit Shastras — that the extreme practices imposed on high-caste widows were, like sati, not required by the scriptural texts in the way the priests claimed. She travelled to England in 1883 to study medicine, encountered the Anglican sisterhood of Wantage, read the New Testament in Marathi, and became a Christian in 1883. She then went to America, delivered lectures on the condition of Indian women, published The High-Caste Hindu Woman in 1887, and raised enough funds to return and act.

Her Sharada Sadan (House of Learning) in Bombay, opened in 1889, was the first institution in India specifically designed to receive high-caste widows and provide them with education, practical skills, and the right to live as human beings rather than as permanent penitents. She rescued widows from across Maharashtra. During the great famines of 1896–97, she organised a caravan of ox carts and travelled personally through the devastated villages of Maharashtra, gathering widows and orphan girls abandoned in the wreckage and bringing them to the Mukti Mission at Kedgaon. By 1900 she was sheltering 1,500 women and children. She also translated the entire Bible from the original Hebrew and Greek into Marathi — a scholarly undertaking of the first order, completed while running a community of that size. She died in 1922. The Mukti Mission she founded continues to this day.

Primary Agents

  • Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) — Convert 1883; Sharada Sadan (Bombay, 1889); Mukti Mission (Kedgaon, 1896); ox-cart famine rescues; Bible translation from Hebrew and Greek into Marathi; sheltered 1,500+ women
  • Zenana mission women — Documentation of widow conditions in purdah households, advocacy for the 1856 Remarriage Act
  • Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar — Hindu reformer supported by missionary documentation; primary architect of the Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act, 1856

Evil X · Medieval — first documented by foreign travellers c. 14th century

The Juggernaut Deaths — जगन्नाथ

Devotees throwing themselves under the wheels of the great temple chariot of Jagannath at Puri, Odisha, during the annual Rath Yatra procession

1850s Practice curtailed by British administration under sustained missionary advocacy; Company collection of pilgrim tax on the festival also discontinued under Christian lobbying.

The image of the Juggernaut — the massive temple chariot of lord Jagannath at Puri, crushing devotees who threw themselves beneath its wheels — entered the English language and became the origin of the word used to describe any overwhelming, unstoppable force. The practice, documented by the medieval traveller Marco Polo and more extensively by later European visitors, involved devotees who believed that death beneath the chariot’s wheels at the moment of a great religious procession guaranteed immediate liberation from the cycle of rebirth. The number who died in any given year was a matter of contested estimate, but the practice was real, the deaths were documented, and the spectacle of it was witnessed by missionaries and recorded in their journals.

Baptist pastor James Peggs was the most persistent campaigner against what he documented in his 1830 work India’s Cries to British Humanity. He also exposed — and this proved the more politically potent argument — that the East India Company was directly profiting from the Jagannath festival: collecting a tax on pilgrims who attended, and using the proceeds for the Company’s revenues. Christian missionaries in Britain and India made the Company’s complicity in a practice that resulted in deaths a matter of sustained political embarrassment. The pilgrim tax was discontinued under missionary pressure. The practice of deliberate self-immolation beneath the chariot wheels was curtailed through administrative intervention in the 1850s, though the festival itself continues as one of India’s great religious processions.

Primary Agents

  • James Peggs — Baptist; India’s Cries to British Humanity (1830); exposed Company tax collection from the Jagannath pilgrimage
  • Baptist Missionary Society press — Sustained Parliamentary campaign; discontinuation of pilgrim tax achieved through Christian lobbying

A Word About the Revisionist Counter-Argument

There is a revisionist account, gaining ground in certain intellectual spaces in contemporary India, that frames the missionary campaign against these practices as an exercise in colonial aggression — a cultural imperialist project that weaponised the suffering of Indian women and tribal communities in order to justify conquest and conversion. The argument is that by exaggerating or sensationalising sati, the Juggernaut deaths, and Meriah sacrifice, Christian missionaries gave the colonial project a moral cover it did not deserve. The conclusion drawn is that the missionaries’ motives were suspect, and therefore their contribution to reform was either illusory or harmful.

The argument deserves a direct answer, not a dismissal. It is true that the line between genuine moral concern and cultural condescension is not always cleanly drawn, but these are legitimate undeniable historical observations.

What the revisionist argument cannot explain is the following: William Carey witnessed a widow burning in 1799 and spent thirty years fighting to stop it, at no personal benefit to himself in any material sense. Amy Carmichael received a branded seven-year-old girl in 1901 and spent the next fifty years building a community to protect her and those like her, at a cost of her health, her homeland, and ultimately her mobility, dying in the country she had made her home. Pandita Ramabai drove ox carts through famine-devastated villages gathering widows and orphans and sheltered 1,500 of them at her own institution. John Campbell spent thirteen years in the forests of Odisha extracting children from human sacrifice networks. The Nadar Christian women of Travancore wore upper garments in the street and had them torn from their bodies, and put them back on, and came back the next day.

These were not the actions of people constructing a pretext. They were the actions of people who had read the Sermon on the Mount and the twenty-fifth chapter of Matthew — inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me — and taken it literally. The gospel they believed was precisely the one that declared liberty to the captive and recovery of sight to the blind, and they acted on it in the bodies and lives of those the world had abandoned.

The dead child in the basket. The woman tied to the pyre. The girl branded on the hand. The purchased boy waiting for the harvest. The woman stripped in the street for wearing a blouse. These were real people. They have no voice in the revisionist argument. The missionaries gave them one, at cost, over decades. That is the record, and it stands.

“Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.” Proverbs 31:8–9 (ESV)

Records, Proceedings on the Age of Consent Bill (1891).

Thuggee: William Henry Sleeman, Ramaseeana (1836); Wikipedia, “Thuggee”; Wikipedia, “Thuggee and Dacoity Department”; GKToday, “Suppression of Thugs by Lord William Bentinck”; Quarterdeck, “William Sleeman: Leadership in the Suppression of Thuggee” (2026).

Breast Tax / Channar Revolt: Wikipedia, “Channar Revolt”; Grokipedia, “Channar Revolt”; LSE eprints, “Christian Missionaries and Female Education in Colonial India”; IJRAR, “Breaking Caste Bonds: The Nadar Community and the Channar Rebellion”; Centre for Law and Policy Research, “The Channar Revolt” (2022).
